---
title: "2. Building and deploying documentation to GitHub Pages"
order: 2
---

In this tutorial you will create documentation for `toymath` using
[Sphinx](https://www.sphinx-doc.org), then write a GitHub Actions workflow
that automatically builds the documentation and publishes it as a website
using [GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages). Every time a change is
merged into `main`, the website will update itself. This is an example of
*continuous deployment*.

This tutorial picks up where [Part 1](tutorial1.qmd) left off. You should
have your fork of `toymath` cloned to your computer, with the `tests.yml` and
`pylint.yml` workflows merged into `main`.

## I. Create the documentation

### 1. Set up a branch and install Sphinx

1.  In your terminal, `cd` into your `toymath` repository and activate the
    environment you created in Part 1:

    ```bash
    conda activate toymath
    ```

2.  Make sure your `main` branch is up to date with your fork on GitHub, then
    create a new branch to work on:

    ```bash
    git checkout main
    git pull
    git checkout -b add-docs
    ```

3.  Install Sphinx:

    ```bash
    pip install sphinx
    ```

    (As with `pytest`, `sphinx` is also listed in the optional dependencies in
    `pyproject.toml`, under `docs`. So you could have instead run
    `pip install -e ".[docs]"`.)

### 2. Run `sphinx-quickstart`

Sphinx comes with a program called `sphinx-quickstart` that sets up the files
you need to get started. From the top level of your repository, run:

```bash
sphinx-quickstart docs
```

This will create a directory called `docs` and put the documentation files
in it. `sphinx-quickstart` will ask you a few questions. Answer them as
follows:

-   `Separate source and build directories (y/n) [n]:` Just hit Enter to
    accept the default (`n`).
-   `Project name:` type `toymath`
-   `Author name(s):` type your name
-   `Project release []:` type `0.1.0` (this is the version of `toymath`
    listed in `pyproject.toml`)
-   `Project language [en]:` Just hit Enter to accept the default (English).

When it finishes, run `ls docs`. You should see:

```bash
Makefile    _build      _static     _templates  conf.py     index.rst   make.bat
```

The two files we care about are:

-   `conf.py`: Sphinx's configuration file. Take a look at it. It's a Python
    file that sets things like the project name and the
    [theme](https://sphinx-themes.org/) to use for the website.
-   `index.rst`: The front page of your documentation. Sphinx uses
    [reStructuredText](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/restructuredtext/basics.html)
    (`.rst`) files by default, which are similar to Markdown files, but with a
    slightly different syntax.

### 3. Add some content

Open `docs/index.rst` in your favorite text editor. Just after the title
(which is underlined with `===`), add a short description of the package so
that the top of the file reads:

```rst
toymath documentation
=====================

``toymath`` is a toy Python package that adds and subtracts numbers.
To install it, run ``pip install .`` from the top level of the repository.
```

(Note that in reStructuredText you need to use *double* backticks to format
something as code, rather than the single backticks used in Markdown.) Leave
the rest of the file as it is.

### 4. Build the documentation on your computer

1.  From the top level of your repository, run:

    ```bash
    sphinx-build -M html docs docs/_build
    ```

    This tells Sphinx to build `html` (i.e., a website) from the source files
    in `docs`, and to put the result in `docs/_build`. At the end you should
    see:

    ```bash
    build succeeded.

    The HTML pages are in docs/_build/html.
    ```

    ::: {.callout-note}
    `sphinx-quickstart` also created a `Makefile` (and a `make.bat` file for
    Windows) in `docs`, so you could also build the documentation by running
    `make html` from inside the `docs` directory. We use `sphinx-build`
    directly here since it works the same way on all operating systems.
    :::

2.  Sphinx created a bunch of HTML files in `docs/_build/html`. Open
    `docs/_build/html/index.html` in your web browser. You can do that by
    double-clicking on the file in Finder (Mac) or File Explorer (Windows), or
    by running the following in your terminal:

    * Mac: `open docs/_build/html/index.html`
    * Windows: `start docs/_build/html/index.html`
    * Linux: `xdg-open docs/_build/html/index.html`

    You should see a simple website with the title "toymath documentation" and
    the description you added. You've built a documentation website!

3.  Try changing something in `docs/index.rst`, re-run the `sphinx-build`
    command, then refresh your browser to see the change.

### 5. Commit the documentation

We don't want to commit the files in `docs/_build`. They're generated from
the source files, so anyone can re-create them by running `sphinx-build`.
(And, as we'll see shortly, GitHub Actions will create them for us.)

1.  Tell `git` to ignore the build directory by adding the following line to the
    end of the `.gitignore` file at the top level of your repository:

    ```bash
    _build/
    ```

    Now run `git status`. You should see `.gitignore` as modified, and `docs/`
    as untracked. If you see anything in `docs/_build` listed, double-check
    your `.gitignore`.

2.  Add and commit the changes:

    ```bash
    git add .gitignore docs
    git commit -m "add sphinx documentation"
    ```

## II. Create a workflow to build and deploy the documentation

Now let's have GitHub build the documentation and publish it to a website.
GitHub has a service called [GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages)
that will host a static website for any public repository, for free. By
default, the website for a repository lives at
`https://YOUR_USERNAME.github.io/REPOSITORY_NAME/`.

### 6. Turn on GitHub Pages

First, we need to tell GitHub that we want to publish a website for our fork,
and that we'll use GitHub Actions to do it.

1.  Go to your fork on GitHub (`https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/toymath`)
    and click on the `Settings` tab at the top.

2.  Click on `Pages` in the menu on the left.

3.  Under "Build and deployment," click the "Source" drop-down menu and select
    `GitHub Actions`.

That's it! There's nothing to save; GitHub will now wait for a workflow to
give it a website to publish.

### 7. Write the workflow

Use your favorite text editor to create a file called
`.github/workflows/docs.yml` and put the following in it:

```yaml
name: Docs

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Check out the repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.13"

      - name: Install Sphinx
        run: |
          python -m pip install --upgrade pip
          pip install sphinx

      - name: Build the documentation
        run: sphinx-build -M html docs docs/_build

      - name: Upload the website
        uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with:
          path: docs/_build/html

  deploy:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      pages: write
      id-token: write
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
        id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5
```

There's a lot here. Let's go through it.

-   **`on`**: This is the same as our `tests.yml` workflow: the workflow will
    run on every pull request, and every time something is pushed to `main`.

-   **The `build` job**: The first few steps should look familiar. We check
    out the repository, install Python, then install Sphinx. We then build the
    documentation using the same `sphinx-build` command you ran on your
    computer. The last step uses the `actions/upload-pages-artifact` action to
    package up the website in `docs/_build/html` and save it.

    ::: {.callout-note}
    Remember that every job runs on a fresh computer. When a job ends, the
    computer is thrown away, along with any files that were created on it! If
    you want to keep a file created by a job, you have to save it as an
    *artifact*. Artifacts are stored by GitHub after the job is done, and can
    be passed to other jobs or downloaded (you'll see them listed at the
    bottom of a workflow's page on the `Actions` tab).
    `actions/upload-pages-artifact` saves the website as a specially formatted
    artifact that GitHub Pages knows how to publish.
    :::

-   **The `deploy` job**: This job takes the artifact created by the `build`
    job and publishes it to GitHub Pages using the `actions/deploy-pages`
    action. There are a few new things here:

    * `needs: build` tells GitHub that this job depends on the `build` job.
      By default, all the jobs in a workflow run at the same time. With
      `needs`, the `deploy` job won't start until `build` finishes, and it
      won't run at all if `build` fails.
    * `if: github.event_name == 'push'` tells GitHub to only run this job if
      the workflow was triggered by a push (i.e., to `main`). When the workflow
      is triggered by a pull request, the `build` job will still run (which
      checks that the documentation builds without errors), but the `deploy`
      job will be skipped. We don't want to publish the website until the
      changes are merged!
    * `permissions` gives the job permission to publish to GitHub Pages.
      Workflows have very limited permissions by default; you have to
      explicitly ask for anything beyond reading the repository.
    * `environment` tells GitHub that this job deploys to the `github-pages`
      environment, which GitHub created when you turned on Pages in the last
      step. The `url` will be shown on the workflow's page, so you can click
      straight through to your website.

### 8. Commit, push, and open a pull request

1.  Commit the workflow and push your branch to your fork:

    ```bash
    git add .github/workflows/docs.yml
    git commit -m "add workflow to build and deploy docs"
    git push -u origin add-docs
    ```

2.  Go to your fork on GitHub and click `Compare & pull request`. **As in
    Part 1, change the base repository to `YOUR_USERNAME/toymath`**, so that
    you're merging `add-docs` into the `main` branch of *your* fork, not the
    upstream repository. Then click `Create pull request`.

3.  Scroll to the bottom of the pull request and look at the checks. You'll
    see the nine `Tests` checks from Part 1, along with
    `Docs / build (pull_request)` and `Docs / deploy (pull_request)`. Once
    they finish, `Docs / build` should pass, and `Docs / deploy` should say
    "Skipped," since this is a pull request, not a push to `main`.

## III. Fixing a failed check

### 9. Pylint is unhappy

You'll also see the `Pylint` checks. Unlike the others, they should have
failed! Click on one of them and expand the "Analysing the code with pylint"
step. You'll see something like:

```bash
************* Module conf
docs/conf.py:1:0: C0114: Missing module docstring (missing-module-docstring)
docs/conf.py:10:0: W0622: Redefining built-in 'copyright' (redefined-builtin)
docs/conf.py:9:0: C0103: Constant name "project" doesn't conform to UPPER_CASE naming style (invalid-name)
...
Your code has been rated at 6.50/10
```

What happened? Our Pylint workflow runs on every Python file in the
repository, and `docs/conf.py` is a Python file. The `conf.py` that
`sphinx-quickstart` created doesn't follow all of Pylint's style rules. Pylint
doesn't like that it doesn't have a docstring; that it uses lowercase names for
variables defined at the top of a module (Pylint thinks these should be
`UPPER_CASE`, since they look like constants); and that it defines a variable
called `copyright`, which is the name of a built-in Python function.

This is exactly what CI is for: catching problems that you didn't notice on
your own computer. In this case the "problems" are with style, not
correctness, and Sphinx requires the variables in `conf.py` to have the names
they do. So rather than renaming the variables, we'll tell Pylint to skip
those particular checks for this file.

1.  Open `docs/conf.py` in your favorite text editor and add the following
    two lines to the very top of the file:

    ```python
    """Configuration file for the Sphinx documentation builder."""
    # pylint: disable=invalid-name,redefined-builtin
    ```

    The first line adds a module docstring. The second is a special comment
    that tells Pylint to ignore the `invalid-name` and `redefined-builtin`
    checks for this file.

2.  If you'd like to check this on your computer before pushing, install
    Pylint and run it the same way the workflow does:

    ```bash
    pip install pylint
    pylint $(git ls-files '*.py')
    ```

    You should get a rating of 10.00/10.

3.  Commit and push the fix:

    ```bash
    git add -u
    git commit -m "fix pylint errors in docs/conf.py"
    git push
    ```

4.  Go back to your pull request and wait for the checks to finish. This time
    they should all pass (with `Docs / deploy` skipped).

## IV. Merge and see the result

### 10. Merge the pull request

1.  Merge the pull request (either a normal merge or a squash and merge is fine
    here), then delete the `add-docs` branch on GitHub.

2.  Click on the `Actions` tab, then click on the latest run of the `Docs`
    workflow. Since merging the pull request pushed to `main`, this time
    *both* jobs will run: first `build`, then `deploy`. You'll see a diagram
    showing the `build` job connected to the `deploy` job by a line. That's
    the `needs: build` at work.

3.  Once the `deploy` job finishes, a link to your website will appear under
    the `deploy` box in the diagram. Click on it (or go to
    `https://YOUR_USERNAME.github.io/toymath/`). You should see the same
    documentation that you built on your own computer, now published on the
    web for anyone to see!

::: {.callout-tip}
To make your documentation easy to find, add a link to it on your
repository's front page. Go to your fork's main page on GitHub, click the
gear icon next to "About" on the right, check the box that says "Use your
GitHub Pages website," then click `Save changes`.
:::

### 11. Sync your local repository

Finally, update your local repository so that it has the merged changes:

```bash
git checkout main
git pull
git branch -D add-docs
```

From now on, any time you update the documentation and merge it into `main`,
your website will update itself automatically. Try it out: make a change to
`docs/index.rst` on a new branch, open a pull request, merge it, and watch
your website change.

::: {.callout-note}
The documentation we created here is very minimal. Real projects use Sphinx
extensions like
[autodoc](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/extensions/autodoc.html)
to generate documentation for every function in the package automatically
from their docstrings, and add pages with installation instructions,
tutorials, and examples. We talked about these in the [packaging and
deployment lecture](../04_packaging_deployment/index.qmd). Since the workflow
just runs `sphinx-build`, all of that would be published to your website too.
:::
